LESSON 33 OF 106·Cryptography Essentials

Common Crypto Failures and How They Become Real

The recurring classes of cryptographic failure — obsolete primitives, missing authentication, downgrades and implementation bugs — and how each one turns into an incident.

Foundation2 min
Why this matters

Cryptographic code fails in recurring ways, and the failures are rarely in the mathematics. They are in the choices around it: what is encrypted, what is verified, and what is compared.

INTERACTIVE FLOW MODEL

  1. Source: Encrypting without authenticating lets an attacker modify the ciphertext, so a decryption failure must stop the application rather than be ignored.
  2. Boundary: The system processes well-formed input along the intended happy path.
  3. Outcome: State transitions and responses remain within expected operational bounds.
01 Untrusted Input

02 Unchecked Assumption
Unblocked
03 Boundary Bypass
  1. Vector: An attacker or faulty client alters parameters, headers, timing, or sequence order.
  2. Weakness: Confirm every message is verified before it is trusted, and that verification failure stops processing.
  3. Impact: The component trusts unverified data, crossing a confidentiality or integrity boundary.
01 Untrusted Input
Enforced control
02 Server Policy Gate
Verified
03 Verified Operation
  1. Verification: Authenticate before you act on data, and treat any verification error as fatal.
  2. Enforcement: Checks run deterministically on the server side for every sensitive action.
  3. Resilience: Invalid requests fail closed and emit structured security telemetry.

What you'll learn

By the end of this lesson you can:

  • confirm every message is verified before it is trusted, and that verification failure stops processing
  • look for ordinary equality comparisons on anything secret, including tokens and session identifiers
  • check that error paths fail closed rather than falling back to an allowed state
  • check algorithm and key length choices against current guidance rather than against what the library defaults to years ago

How it works

  • Encrypting without authenticating lets an attacker modify the ciphertext, so a decryption failure must stop the application rather than be ignored.
  • Comparing values with an ordinary string comparison can leak the correct value through timing, so secret comparisons must be constant time.
  • Padding oracles let an attacker learn about plaintext from error behaviour, which is why modern schemes avoid them or make errors indistinguishable.
  • Inventing a construction from sound primitives can still be insecure, because a scheme is more than the sum of its parts.
  • Failing open on an error, such as accepting traffic when verification is unavailable, turns a security control into an availability preference.

The background

  • Early application code decrypted and then trusted the result, so errors were informative by default.
  • A long series of padding oracle vulnerabilities demonstrated that error handling alone can break an otherwise sound scheme.
  • High-level libraries absorbed many of these lessons, and the residual failures are now mostly in how applications use them.
  • Framework guidance now forbids rolling your own crypto in most languages for exactly this reason.

Real-world examples

  • A verification error that is logged and then ignored lets an attacker tamper with signed data without anyone noticing.
  • A timing side channel on a token comparison is difficult to notice and difficult to fix once shipped.
  • Using a fast hash for signatures with a short key length reduces the scheme to something that can be brute forced.

What to look for

  • Confirm every message is verified before it is trusted, and that verification failure stops processing.
  • Look for ordinary equality comparisons on anything secret, including tokens and session identifiers.
  • Check that error paths fail closed rather than falling back to an allowed state.
  • Check algorithm and key length choices against current guidance rather than against what the library defaults to years ago.

Practice / apply

Use a suitable learning environment and follow the resource's instructions. Test other people's systems only with permission.

Key takeaways

  • Authenticate before you act on data, and treat any verification error as fatal.
  • Use constant-time comparison functions provided by the platform rather than writing your own.
  • Never invent a construction; choose a named, reviewed one and use it as documented.
  • Keep libraries updated, because most crypto failures live in code that has not been revised.
  • Have cryptographic choices reviewed by someone who did not write the feature.
